results.result: The study reanalyzed data from Bakkour et al., 2019, in which 30 participants completed a food choice task. Participants first rated 60 snack items on willingness to pay ($0-$3), then made binary choices between pairs of items in 210 trials (each item appearing 7 times, with 60 pairs repeated once). The experimental procedures were approved by the IRB at Columbia University.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C55-C56, and C102-C109 provide consistent and detailed descriptions of the experimental design, sample size, and procedures. These are straightforward methodological details that are internally consistent and appropriately documented.

results.result: Participants chose the item with higher static value (s-value) in only 64% of trials, and overall behavior was similar to other studies using the same task.
results.evaluation: Claim C3 provides a specific quantitative result (64% choice consistency), and C8 contextualizes this within the literature. The low consistency rate is a key observation motivating the study's hypothesis about dynamic values.

results.result: Participants were more likely to select the same option when presentations of identical pairs were closer in time, with a highly significant negative regression coefficient (p<0.0001) for the number of trials between repetitions. This demonstrates that preferences are not fixed even within a single experimental session.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11 present converging evidence from repeated-pair analysis with appropriate statistical testing (Figure 3, Equation 8). The inference in C11 logically follows from the temporal dependency shown in C9-C10.

results.result: A regression model using choices from other trials predicted cynosure trial choices better than a model using explicitly reported static values (s-values). Explicit value reports have limited power to predict choices, and the values used to make binary choices differ from and drift apart from s-values during the experiment through the deliberative process.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by the model comparison in Figure 2 and control simulations. The superiority of the choice-based model over s-values is demonstrated empirically, and the interpretation about value drift (C62-C63) follows logically from these results.

results.result: Dynamic values (d-values) derived from the Reval algorithm explain choices and response times better than explicit value reports (s-values). The DDM using d-values explained more RT variance, provided better fits for all participants (by BIC), and better classified trial difficulty.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C17 present multiple converging lines of evidence (Figures 5, 5-supplement 2) showing d-values outperform s-values in explaining both choice and RT data. The BIC comparison (C16) appropriately penalizes the additional parameter in the dynamic model.

results.result: Control analyses using simulated data showed that the improvements in fit quality from applying Reval are neither guaranteed nor artifactual. The reduction in deviance after applying Reval was negligible in simulated data compared to actual data.
results.evaluation: Claims C19 and C69 describe critical control analyses (Figure 6) that rule out the possibility that Reval improvements are methodological artifacts. The simulations appropriately test the null hypothesis that values are static.

results.result: Reval applied in the correct (forward) temporal order explained choices significantly better than when applied in reverse order (p<0.0001), ruling out the possibility that values are static. This effect cannot be explained by the Chen and Risen (2010) artifact. Surprisingly, backward Reval still explained choices better than static values.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C21 and C68-C74 present the forward-backward comparison (Figure 7) that provides strong evidence against static values. The logical reasoning in C68 is sound, and the results directly address the Chen and Risen artifact concern. The backward-better-than-static result (C21) is unexpected but explained by the ceDDM model.

results.result: For most participants, revaluation was greater for chosen than unchosen items. This asymmetry may relate to unequal attention distribution, as chosen items are looked at longer and the ceDDM predicts larger revaluation with more evidence samples.
results.evaluation: Claim C23 presents the empirical finding (Figure 8), while C70 and C84-C87 provide mechanistic speculation supported by prior literature and model predictions. The asymmetric revaluation is a robust empirical observation, though the mechanistic explanation remains speculative.

results.result: fMRI analysis revealed that vmPFC BOLD signal correlated significantly with d-values when controlling for s-values. A model with only s-values did not survive whole-brain correction in vmPFC, while a model with only d-values showed robust vmPFC effects surviving correction.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 present fMRI results (Figure 9, Figure 9-supplement 1) with appropriate whole-brain correction. The differential effects of d-values vs s-values in vmPFC provide neural evidence supporting the behavioral findings. However, the fMRI analysis would benefit from more detail about potential confounds and the specificity of the vmPFC effect.

results.result: Reval was applied to three independent datasets (Folke et al. 2016; Sepulveda et al. 2020 like-framing and dislike-framing), yielding largely similar results. The reduction in deviance was significantly greater than in simulated data for all three datasets. Forward-backward differences replicated in Folke et al. but not in Sepulveda et al., possibly due to alternating instruction blocks.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C33 and C91 describe replication analyses (Figure 10) across independent datasets. The partial replication strengthens confidence in the main findings, while the failure in one dataset (C33) is acknowledged and speculatively explained (C91). The mixed results suggest boundary conditions for the effect.

results.result: The correlated-evidence drift-diffusion model (ceDDM) successfully captured the revaluation effects. After 1s of evidence sampling, correlation was 0.1062±0.0113. When Reval was applied to ceDDM simulations, it increased RT range by difficulty, explained choices better in forward than backward direction, and backward Reval outperformed static values—mirroring empirical patterns. This supports the interpretation that revaluation reflects dynamic value construction during deliberation.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39 and C71-C72 present the ceDDM modeling results (Figure 11) showing the model can reproduce key empirical patterns. The model provides a mechanistic account of how temporally correlated evidence samples can generate revaluation-like effects. However, C80 and C92 appropriately note this is a proof-of-principle model.

results.result: The manuscript establishes theoretical context: value-based decisions are thought to rely on comparing subjective values, with longer RTs for similar values. However, unlike perceptual decisions where evidence samples are conditionally independent, value-based decisions may involve dynamic, context-dependent valuations influenced by decision-maker mindset, which can be persistent or shift rapidly.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C51 provide theoretical background and motivation. These are primarily literature review and conceptual framing rather than novel empirical claims. The critical assessment in C46 that conditional independence is questionable for value-based decisions is the key conceptual contribution motivating the study.

results.result: The authors hypothesized that if subjective values are dynamic, value-based decisions should exhibit serial dependencies. A choice provides information about the decision-maker's mindset, which likely endures longer than a single decision, making choices informative about future choices.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 state the study's central hypothesis and reasoning. This is appropriate hypothesis generation based on the theoretical considerations in the previous result. The hypothesis is clearly testable and motivated.

results.result: The manuscript contrasts two explanations for choice variability: the standard view attributes it to noise in memory retrieval, while constructive value theories suggest values are constructed (not retrieved) during decisions and are sensitive to context.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 present competing theoretical frameworks from the literature. This framing appropriately contextualizes the study's contribution within ongoing theoretical debates about value representation.

results.result: The sequential effects identified can be interpreted as choice-induced preference change (CIPC), a phenomenon documented since Festinger (1957) using free-choice paradigms. However, the revaluation effect found here cannot be explained by the Chen and Risen (2010) artifact. The approach does not require pre- and post-choice ratings but instead requires repeated item presentations. The timing of revaluation (during vs after deliberation) cannot be determined with certainty.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C77 situate the findings within the CIPC literature and address methodological concerns. The distinction from the Chen and Risen artifact is well-supported by the forward-backward analysis. The acknowledgment of uncertainty about timing (C77) is appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: The subjective value of options depends on decision-maker mindset; if mindset changes are slow, item values will be temporally correlated. The ceDDM is interpreted as a proxy for nuanced processes and belongs to a class of sequential sampling models with time-varying drift rates, similar to attentional DDM and models by Lee and Pezzulo (2022).
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C83 provide theoretical interpretation and model contextualization. The acknowledgment that ceDDM is a proxy (C80) is important scientific humility. The connection to related models (C81-C83) appropriately situates the work.

results.result: The study has several acknowledged limitations: it only examined food items with explicit value reports, generalization to other value elicitation methods and non-food items remains to be determined, perceptual decisions also show serial dependencies that may or may not reflect similar processes, and alternative stochastic processes or mechanisms (beyond past decisions) might also explain the observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C94 appropriately acknowledge study limitations and boundary conditions. These are reasonable caveats that do not undermine the main findings but identify important directions for future research.

results.result: The research contributes to understanding memory's impact on decision-making and preference formation. Prior work suggests value retrieval renders items susceptible to modification (Luettgau et al. 2020), and mere exposure increases preference (Zajonc 1968). Due to memory's associative nature, successive evidence samples are likely dependent, similar to Lévy flights in semantic space (Costa et al. 2009) and foraging behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C101 provide broader context and connections to related phenomena. These appropriately situate the work within cognitive science and suggest interesting parallels to other domains, though the connections remain somewhat speculative (C101).

results.result: The authors demonstrate that preferences are not fixed during a single experimental session. Participants were more likely to select the same option when presentations of the same pair were closer in time, with a highly significant negative regression coefficient (p<0.0001) for the number of trials between repetitions.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers affirm the core finding that subjective values change across sequences of decisions. The editor states the authors 'provide convincing evidence that the subjective values human participants assign to items change across sequences of multiple decisions,' and reviewers explicitly note the authors 'clearly demonstrate this re-evaluation phenomenon in several existing datasets.'

results.result: The Reval algorithm produces dynamic values (d-values) that explain choices and response times better than static values (s-values). The DDM using d-values provided better fits for all participants, explained more variance in RT, and better classified easy vs. difficult trials.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm that 'estimations of dynamic valuation correlate with neural activity' and that the evidence is 'solid.' One reviewer states 'food choice outcomes and BOLD signal in the vmPFC are better explained by algorithms that update subjective values during the sequence of choices compared to algorithms based on static values.' The methods are described as 'novel' and 'robust.'

results.result: Control analyses demonstrate that improvements from Reval are not artifacts. The reduction in deviance was negligible in simulated data, variance explained was greater when Reval was applied in the correct temporal order (p<0.0001), and even backward Reval explained choices better than static values.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note that 'the authors provided evidence for the behaviour effect using several techniques and generated surrogate data (where the ground truth is known) to demonstrate the robustness of their methods.' The control analyses are treated as convincing validation of the main findings.

results.result: fMRI analysis revealed that vmPFC BOLD signal significantly correlated with d-values (controlling for s-values), and d-values alone showed robust effects surviving whole-brain correction, while s-values alone did not survive correction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'estimations of dynamic valuation correlate with neural activity in prefrontal cortex' and that 'BOLD signal in the vmPFC are better explained by algorithms that update subjective values.' The neural evidence is treated as supporting the behavioral findings without critique.

results.result: Reval was applied to three independent datasets with largely similar results. The reduction in deviance was significantly greater than simulated data in all datasets. Forward vs. backward Reval showed significant differences in Folke et al. (2016) but not in Sepulveda et al. (2020).
results.evaluation: Reviewers note the authors 'clearly demonstrate this re-evaluation phenomenon in several existing datasets,' treating the replication as evidence of robustness. The mixed result in one dataset (C33) is acknowledged by the authors as potentially due to experimental design idiosyncrasies (C91), and reviewers do not challenge this interpretation.

results.result: A novel correlated-evidence drift-diffusion model (ceDDM) with temporally correlated evidence samples reproduces key behavioral patterns. The model shows correlation of 0.1062±0.0113 after 1s, and when Reval is applied to ceDDM simulations, it increases RT range by difficulty, explains choices better in forward than backward direction, and mirrors patterns in real data.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the ceDDM as a 'novel' contribution and note the authors 'generated surrogate data (where the ground truth is known) to demonstrate the robustness of their methods.' The modeling work is treated as supporting the interpretation that revaluation reflects dynamic value construction during deliberation.

results.result: For most participants, revaluation is greater for chosen than unchosen items, which is consistent with chosen items being attended longer and the ceDDM prediction that correlation decreases with evidence sampling.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this asymmetric revaluation finding. It is presented as consistent with established attention patterns and model predictions, and reviewers affirm the overall evidence as 'solid' without raising concerns about this specific result.

results.result: The sequential effects can be interpreted as choice-induced preference change (CIPC), cannot be explained by the Chen and Risen (2010) artifact, and the approach does not require pre- and post-choice ratings but instead requires repeated item presentations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state 'there is a long-standing idea that choices influence evaluation' and affirm the authors 'clearly demonstrate this re-evaluation phenomenon.' The methodological advantages and distinction from prior artifacts are not questioned by reviewers.

results.result: Participants chose the higher s-value item in only 64% of trials, showing behavior similar to other studies. A regression model using choices from other trials is superior to s-values for predicting choices, demonstrating that explicit value reports have limited predictive power.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question these basic behavioral observations. They are treated as establishing the context for the main findings about dynamic values. The comparison to prior studies and the limited predictive power of static values are accepted without critique.

results.result: The authors acknowledge several limitations: the study only examined food items with explicit value reports, other elicitation methods remain to be tested, perceptual decisions may show similar patterns, the Sepulveda dataset failure may relate to experimental design, and alternative stochastic processes might explain the observations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise the authors for 'avoid[ing] over-selling the work, with a lucid description of limitations, and potential for further exploration of the work, in the discussion.' The acknowledgment of limitations is treated as a strength rather than undermining the main findings. One reviewer notes the evidence is 'currently limited to choices between food items because no other goods were examined.'

results.result: The study re-examined data from Bakkour et al. (2019) with 30 participants who rated 60 snack items ($0-$3) and completed 210 trials with each item appearing seven times. The experimental procedures included rating revision opportunities, specific trial timing (500ms confirmation, exponential ITI distribution with mean 3.05s), and IRB approval.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question the methodological details or experimental design. The reanalysis of existing data is accepted, and reviewers note the methods are 'well-written' with 'clear' figures. The experimental procedures are treated as appropriate for addressing the research questions.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on methodological claims (C1, C2, C55, C56, C102-C109). Both evaluations find the experimental design, sample size, and procedures well-documented and appropriate. Reviewers note methods are 'well-written' with 'clear' figures, aligning with OpenEval's assessment of consistent and detailed documentation.

Perfect agreement on core revaluation finding (C9-C11). Both evaluations affirm the temporal dependency evidence from repeated-pair analysis. Reviewers explicitly state authors 'provide convincing evidence that subjective values change across sequences' and 'clearly demonstrate this re-evaluation phenomenon,' matching OpenEval's assessment of converging evidence with appropriate statistical testing.

Perfect agreement on model comparison claims (C13-C17). Both evaluations support that d-values outperform s-values in explaining choice and RT data. Reviewers describe evidence as 'solid' and methods as 'novel' and 'robust,' affirming that dynamic valuation algorithms better explain outcomes than static value algorithms, consistent with OpenEval's assessment of converging evidence.

Perfect agreement on ceDDM modeling (C35-C39, C71-C72). Both evaluations support the model's ability to reproduce empirical patterns. Reviewers describe ceDDM as 'novel' and note authors 'generated surrogate data to demonstrate robustness,' aligning with OpenEval's assessment that the model provides mechanistic account of revaluation-like effects, though both acknowledge it as proof-of-principle.

Strong agreement on study limitations (C88-C90, C93-C94). Both evaluations treat acknowledgment of limitations as appropriate scientific practice.
